analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars and charge patients less for them than for brand-name drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 21 cosponsors from both parties, never received a committee vote or House floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required Medicare prescription drug plans (the private plans in Part D) to put any generic drug or biosimilar that costs less than its brand-name counterpart on their lists of covered drugs. Plans would also have to charge patients less out-of-pocket for those cheaper versions, and could not make seniors jump through prior-authorization or step-therapy hoops for the generic that they do not impose on the brand-name drug. It never received a vote in either committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees, most of them seniors on fixed incomes. They would have had guaranteed access to cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars on plan formularies, lower cost-sharing for those drugs than for brands, and no extra hoops like prior authorization or step therapy for the generic that the brand drug does not require. Taxpayers would also benefit, since Medicare subsidizes Part D and cheaper dispensing reduces plan costs that flow back into premiums.

how_it_helps.text: It required Medicare drug plans to include on their formularies every generic drug and biosimilar that costs less than the brand-name original.
It barred plans from imposing prior authorization, step therapy, or other access limits on those cheaper generics that are stricter than the limits on the brand-name drugs.
It required plans to create cost-sharing tiers for generics priced meaningfully below the cheapest brand tier, so seniors pay less at the pharmacy counter for the cheaper version.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Part D plan sponsors (private insurers) and, indirectly, brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to steer patients toward higher-priced brand products through formulary placement and cost-sharing. Plans could also face compliance costs in restructuring their formulary tiers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare drug plans and brand-name drugmakers

drawbacks.text: The bill forced plans to put cheaper generics on their formularies with lower cost-sharing even when a brand drug had a negotiated rebate, which plans and brand manufacturers argued could raise premiums or narrow other benefits to cover the difference.
The Secretary would have had to define terms like 'meaningfully lesser' cost-sharing, creating regulatory discretion and compliance costs for plan sponsors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—cheaper, easier access to generics and biosimilars for Medicare beneficiaries—would have come at a real cost to drug plans and brand-name manufacturers, who would have lost tools to steer patients to higher-priced brand products. Those tools exist partly because of rebates plans receive from brands, so the bill's designers accepted some friction with plan economics in exchange for lower out-of-pocket costs at the pharmacy counter. It was never voted on, so the trade was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a vote in either, and expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley introduced the bill on October 30, 2019, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and to a Health Subcommittee.
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The bill drew 21 cosponsors split between 12 Democrats and 9 Republicans, but the committee chairmen never scheduled it for consideration.
It died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare drug plan sponsors and brand-name drug makers keep the ability to steer patients toward higher-priced brand-name drugs; seniors keep paying brand-name-level cost-sharing where plans prefer it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 21 cosponsors split 12 Democrats and 9 Republicans, showing support across both parties, though neither party's leadership moved it.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plan sponsors (insurers)
industries.note: The bill forced plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars, charge less for them, and not steer patients toward brand-name drugs, reducing their flexibility and some rebate-driven revenue. Its death preserved the status quo.
Plans could no longer give brand drugs preferred status over cheaper generics and biosimilars, cutting into brand-name sales in Medicare Part D. The bill's failure kept that advantage intact.
Guaranteed formulary inclusion and lower cost-sharing would have driven more prescriptions toward generic and biosimilar products. The bill never passed, so the gain never materialized.
